title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 4: Advice for Aspiring Attorneys
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'Justice and Faith' -- CJP's FEU Institute of Law commencement address giving aspiring attorneys a 'seven-point advice' for starting a legal career, framed by his own 1960 FEU graduation and bar-prep memory thirty-five years earlier

A diagnosis of the Philippine justice delivery system as plagued by delay, citing Fernan's and Narvasa's UP self-assessments and the Multi-Sectoral Conference's October 17, 1992 De La Salle workshop CJP chaired; the 'anak na pinag-awayan' joke as the popular face of that delay

The Flor Contemplacion outrage as sociological proof that Filipinos can bear poverty and hunger but not injustice; 1 in 3 Metro Manila households had a member temporarily abroad per a SWS survey, supplying the rage

A practical seven-point program for the new lawyer -- preparation, ADRs (arbitration/mediation), pre-trial cooperation, justice over delay, free legal services for the poor, a stand-by philosophy of law, and surrender to God -- each presented as a discrete actionable principle

The closing theological frame from Philippians 3:8-9 and Matthew 25 -- the letter-versus-spirit distinction, and the ultimate question we will be asked at judgment ('Did you feed the hungry, clothe the naked...?') as the synthesizing yardstick for a legal career
sub_topics: Judge Clemente M. Soriano introduction and CJP's tribute to him as 'the first law student to be elected president of the FEU Central Student Organization,' the post CJP himself later attained
'FEU is the best law school' tease vs. the unnamed cabinet member's UP rejoinder -- CJP turns the joke: 'They are the reality; we are the promise'
Bar-prep mechanics from CJP's own 1960 experience -- multi-lined Grade I pad paper for legible handwriting, six hours of sleep / eighteen hours of study, English review with his professor

The FEU tutorial system: top ten of the last three bar exams tutoring the current 'magic 20' candidates; CJP's own hospitalization on day 1 of the bar at FEU Hospital, walking to UE through flooded streets

FEU bar-topnotcher law-firm legacy -- Salonga's invitation post-1960, then CJP's own partnership with Benitez (No. 1, 1959), Parlade (No. 4, 1959), Africa (No. 1, 1960) and later Sylvia Katherine Luczon-Barinaga (No. 5, 1968)
Fernan's 'court congestion and litigation delay' lecture (UP) and Narvasa's March 10, 1992 UP self-assessment with 338,517 filings roughly equaling dispositions in the lower courts
The Multi-Sectoral Conference on the Administration of Justice at De La Salle, October 17, 1992, CJP as chairman -- a thousand-day program for the Ramos administration noting growing backlog

Quality and corruption as the parallel complaints -- clients ask 'Do you know the judge?' before 'Is my case meritorious?'; National Unification Commission survey naming INJUSTICE alongside POVERTY, CRIMINALITY, CORRUPTION

The seven-point advice spelled out one by one with concrete operational content (e.g., ADRs and the ICC seminar with Louise Barrington, Stephen Bond, and CJP as resource lecturers; IBP free legal assistance and PPCRV/NAMFREL as volunteering venues)

Justice Isagani R. Cruz quotation on the SC as 'the conscience of the government' -- law and justice are not always the same; closing fusion with Philippians and Matthew 25 to recast the practical program as a theological ethic

stances.claim: Slow, expensive justice -- clogged dockets, lawyerly delay tactics, perceived corruption -- is the deepest popular grievance against the legal system; lawyers are the wound-carers of that grievance.
stances.rhetorical_move: diagnostic-then-vocational: cite Fernan, Narvasa, the NUC survey, and the Contemplacion outrage, then place the new lawyer as the one called to heal it

stances.claim: Filipinos can endure poverty and hunger but cannot endure injustice -- the Flor Contemplacion outrage proves this, magnified by the SWS finding that 1 in 3 Metro Manila households had a member abroad.
stances.rhetorical_move: sociological-evidence: rage is decoded as solidarity with absent OFW kin, not abstract idealism

stances.claim: Aspiring lawyers should embrace ADRs (arbitration and mediation) and pre-trial cooperation as professional virtues -- not as concessions, but as the modern lucrative specialty (e.g., ICC international contracts) and as respect for the court's time.
stances.rhetorical_move: career-counsel: turns a public-policy reform into a personal opportunity

stances.claim: Law and justice are not always identical; the legitimate aim of legal technique is to make truth and justice prevail, never to abuse rules to win at any cost -- the Cruz ponencia is the standard.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-anchoring: borrow Cruz to gird an ethical exhortation

stances.claim: Every lawyer should develop and stand by a philosophy of law -- because in practice S × P = D (stimuli × personality = decision), not Law × Facts = Decision; predicting judges and being a judge yourself requires this self-knowledge.
stances.rhetorical_move: realist-jurisprudence: Holmes / Pound / Concepcion invoked as exemplars

stances.claim: Helping the poor for free yields rewards money cannot buy -- CJP's first criminal acquittal (a penniless rape defendant) brought a fulfillment more intense than the Banco Filipino SC victory.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-testimony: a benchmark comparison that ranks pro-bono joy above commercial triumph

stances.claim: The ultimate yardstick of a legal career is Matthew 25 -- whether the lawyer used profession and possessions to defend the weak and the poor; bar rank, fees, titles and offices are irrelevant at that final accounting.
stances.rhetorical_move: eschatological-closure: collapses six secular advices into one theological question

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's FEU Institute of Law commencement address (c. 1995), introduced by his former FEUCSO predecessor Judge Clemente M. Soriano and hosted by Dean Justice Oscar R. Victoriano. CJP returns to 'the green and gold portals' thirty-five years after his own 1960 graduation, recounting his Salonga-tutored bar-prep, hospitalization on day one of the 1960 exams, and the FEU-bar-topnotcher pedigree that later produced his Panganiban-Benitez-Parlade-Africa-Barinaga law firm. The body of the speech diagnoses the Philippine justice system's deepest grievance -- clogged dockets and lawyerly delay tactics -- quoting Chief Justices Marcelo B. Fernan and Andres R. Narvasa's UP self-assessments and the Multi-Sectoral Conference on the Administration of Justice CJP chaired at De La Salle on October 17, 1992; the 'anak na pinag-awayan' courtroom joke supplies the popular face of that delay, while the Flor Contemplacion outrage (decoded against a SWS finding that 1 in 3 Metro Manila households had a member abroad) supplies the moral. CJP then gives the graduates a seven-point advice: improve bar preparation; embrace ADRs (arbitration and mediation, including the ICC's international rules); cooperate with judges through pre-trial admissions; use law to promote justice not to delay it (anchored in retired Justice Isagani R. Cruz's 'conscience of the government' ponencia); volunteer free legal services for the poor (IBP, PPCRV, NAMFREL); develop a personal philosophy of law (S × P = D realism, with Holmes/Pound/Concepcion as exemplars); and finally, surrender to God. He closes by collapsing the six secular advices into the seventh through Philippians 3:8-9 ('not by the letter that killeth but by the spirit that giveth life') and Matthew 25 -- the ultimate question we will be asked at judgment is whether we used possession and profession to defend the weak and the poor, not how many bar honors, millions or titles we collected.
